span.label: A WORKING GROUP DEFINING A CONDITION THAT HAD BEEN NAMED FOR TWENTY-ONE YEARS - four European societies convened to give sarcopenia a clinical definition, diagnostic criteria and cut-off points, because it had none
span.note: Quotation withheld because this record is not cleared for redistribution.

span.label: what sarcopenia is, what parameters define it, which variables measure those parameters, at what cut-off points, and how it relates to cachexia, frailty and sarcopenic obesity
span.note: Quotation withheld because this record is not cleared for redistribution.

span.label: A TERM COINED IN 1989 THAT STILL HAD NO AGREED DEFINITION IN 2010: `In 1989, Irwin Rosenberg proposed the term `SARCOPENIA` (GREEK `SARX` or flesh + `PENIA` or loss) to describe this age-related decrease of muscle mass. Sarcopenia has since been defined as the loss of skeletal muscle mass and strength that occurs with advancing age. However, a widely accepted definition of sarcopenia suitable for use in research and clinical practice is still lacking.` The coinage is dated, attributed and given its etymology, and the gap it left is stated in the next sentence
span.note: Quotation withheld because this record is not cleared for redistribution.

span.label: AND THE ABSENCE IS ENUMERATED, INCLUDING THE ADMINISTRATIVE ONE: `sarcopenia still has no broadly accepted clinical definition, consensus diagnostic criteria, International Classification of Diseases 9th Revision (ICD-9) codes or treatment guidelines.` A missing ICD code is a missing SLOT IN A CONTROLLED VOCABULARY, listed beside the missing definition as the same kind of lack - the clearest statement in this corpus that a definition and its administrative code are one problem
span.note: Quotation withheld because this record is not cleared for redistribution.

span.label: AND A BETTER TERM WAS REJECTED BECAUSE THE WORSE ONE IS ALREADY KNOWN: `Some have argued that the term dynapenia is better suited to describe age-associated loss of muscle strength and function. However, sarcopenia is already a widely recognised term, so replacing it might lead to further confusion.` THE EXACT MIRROR OF haas2018: Banff DELETED the word `acute` because it confused clinicians; EWGSOP KEPT `sarcopenia`, against a term it concedes is better suited, because replacing it would confuse. Two consensus bodies, opposite decisions, the same reason - and neither decision is about the biology
span.note: Quotation withheld because this record is not cleared for redistribution.

span.label: AND THE PREVALENCE RANGE IS ATTRIBUTED TO THE DEFINITION IN ONE SENTENCE: `Depending on the literature definition used for sarcopenia, the prevalence in 60-70-year-olds is reported as 5-13%, while the prevalence ranges from 11 to 50% in people >80 years.` bellomo2004 and hoste2006 each gave a range and left the reader to infer the cause; this paper names it
span.note: Quotation withheld because this record is not cleared for redistribution.

span.label: AND A THRESHOLD SET BY WHAT DATA EXISTED, CALLED ARBITRARY BY THE PAPER ITSELF: `Quotation withheld` The class boundary is where the reference data ran out, and the sentence says which population's absence set it
span.note: Quotation withheld because this record is not cleared for redistribution.

span.label: AND THE CONVENTION BEHIND EVERY OTHER CUT-OFF IS STATED AS A CHOICE: `EWGSOP recommends use of normative (healthy young adult) rather than other predictive reference populations, with cut-off points at two standard deviations below the mean reference value. More research is urgently needed in order to obtain good reference values for populations around the world.` Two decisions - which population is the reference, and how many SDs below it - and the paper concedes the first is under-supplied
span.note: Quotation withheld because this record is not cleared for redistribution.

span.label: AND THE INTENSION IS DECLARED TOO NARROW, WITH THE REASON: `muscle strength does not depend solely on muscle mass, and the relationship between strength and mass is not linear. Thus, defining sarcopenia only in terms of muscle mass is too narrow and may be of limited clinical value.` The two-criterion rule is derived from a non-linearity rather than asserted
span.note: Quotation withheld because this record is not cleared for redistribution.

span.label: and the category is adopted BECAUSE the causes are unknown, not despite it: `We suggest it may be likewise helpful to recognise sarcopenia as a geriatric syndrome because this view promotes its identification and treatment even when the exact causes remain unknown.` A class chosen for what it lets clinicians do, with the aetiological ignorance stated as part of the justification
span.note: Quotation withheld because this record is not cleared for redistribution.

span.label: THE NEIGHBOURING CONSTRUCTS OVERLAP ASYMMETRICALLY AND ONE IS PART OF THE OTHER'S DEFINITION: `most cachectic individuals are also sarcopenic, but most sarcopenic individuals are not considered cachectic. Sarcopenia is one of the elements of the proposed definition for cachexia.` A concept that is a COMPONENT OF ANOTHER CONCEPT'S DEFINITION while also being distinguished from it - the corpus has no edge type for `is part of the definition of`, only for parts of things
span.note: Quotation withheld because this record is not cleared for redistribution.

span.label: AND FRAILTY OVERLAPS IT WHILE EXTENDING BEYOND IT: `Frailty and sarcopenia overlap; most frail older people exhibit sarcopenia, and some older people with sarcopenia are also frail. The general concept of frailty, however, goes beyond physical factors to encompass psychological and social dimensions as well.` Overlap without containment in either direction, said in one sentence
span.note: Quotation withheld because this record is not cleared for redistribution.

span.label: and there is no standard outcome to test a treatment against: `only a handful of clinical trials are under way to test potential sarcopenia treatments. The absence of standardised primary outcomes is a major challenge for the design of such studies.` The definition is proposed so that trials become possible, and the paper says in the same paragraph that the outcomes for those trials do not exist either
span.note: Quotation withheld because this record is not cleared for redistribution.

span.label: and the stages are labelled CONCEPTUAL, with presarcopenia reachable only by an instrument most clinics do not have: `This stage can only be identified by techniques that measure muscle mass accurately and in reference to standard populations` - so the first stage of the classification is, in practice, unobservable wherever the reference populations are the ones the paper says are missing
span.note: Quotation withheld because this record is not cleared for redistribution.

span.label: requiring BOTH low muscle mass and low muscle function for the diagnosis, rather than mass alone
span.note: eliminates: a definition that the paper argues is too narrow, on the grounds that 'muscle strength does not depend solely on muscle mass, and the relationship between strength and mass is not linear' · outcome: held
Quotation withheld because this record is not cleared for redistribution.

span.note: eliminates: cut-off points that drift with whichever study population happens to be at hand · outcome: partial

span.label: `sarcopenia` (Rosenberg 1989) - the COINAGE: Greek `sarx` (flesh) + `penia` (loss), for the age-related decrease of muscle MASS alone
span.note: Quotation withheld because this record is not cleared for redistribution.

span.label: `sarcopenia` (EWGSOP 2010) - MASS PLUS FUNCTION: `a syndrome characterised by progressive and generalised loss of skeletal muscle mass and strength`, diagnosed as `low muscle mass PLUS low muscle strength or low physical performance`. The 1989 sense is declared `too narrow`
span.note: Quotation withheld because this record is not cleared for redistribution.

span.label: `dynapenia` - the term EWGSOP concedes is `better suited to describe age-associated loss of muscle strength and function`, and declines to adopt because `sarcopenia is already a widely recognised term`
span.note: Quotation withheld because this record is not cleared for redistribution.

span.label: `primary` vs `secondary sarcopenia` - the same condition split by whether a cause OTHER THAN AGEING is evident; the paper adds that in many older people the aetiology is multi-factorial so neither label applies
span.note: Quotation withheld because this record is not cleared for redistribution.

span.label: `presarcopenia` / `sarcopenia` / `severe sarcopenia` - three CONCEPTUAL stages by how many of the three criteria are met
span.note: Quotation withheld because this record is not cleared for redistribution.

span.label: extends → Rosenberg's 1989 coinage of 'sarcopenia' for the age-related decrease of muscle mass - this paper keeps the name and widens the intension to require function

span.label: critiques → the literature's definitions of sarcopenia by muscle mass alone, which the paper calls 'too narrow and may be of limited clinical value'

span.label: sarcopenia —distinct-from→ cachexia
span.note: the relation itself is separately evidenced · strength of the relation: 0.95 · note: 'most cachectic…' Distinct, asymmetrically overlapping, and one is a component of the other's DEFINITION - which the schema cannot say, so it is in the note · the relation stated: the overlap runs ONE WAY: most cachectic individuals are sarcopenic, most sarcopenic individuals are not cachectic
Quotation withheld because this record is not cleared for redistribution.

span.label: sarcopenia —is-a→ syndrome
span.note: the relation itself is separately evidenced · strength of the relation: 0.9 · note: Weight 0.9, not 0.95: 'syndrome' is a broad endpoint, and the paper's sharper claim is the narrower class 'GERIATRIC syndrome', argued separately and adopted BECAUSE the causes are unknown - 'this view promotes…' · the relation stated: 'Sarcopenia is a syndrome characterised by ...' - the working definition's own opening clause
Quotation withheld because this record is not cleared for redistribution.

span.label: primary sarcopenia —distinct-from→ secondary sarcopenia
span.note: the relation itself is separately evidenced · strength of the relation: 0.95 · note: `Sarcopenia can be considered `primary` (or age-related) when no other cause is evident but ageing itself, while sarcopenia can be considered `secondary` when one or more other causes are evident.` The split is by AETIOLOGY, not by presentation - and the paper immediately concedes that `in many older people the aetiology is multi-factorial so that it may not be possible to characterise each individual as having a primary or secondary condition` · the relation stated: one condition split by whether a cause OTHER THAN AGEING is evident
Quotation withheld because this record is not cleared for redistribution.
